stimulus.text: Photograph of the signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact at the Quai d'Orsay in Paris, August 27, 1928. A man holds up the open pact for the camera; its pages are covered with signatures, and round seals hang from ribbons down the center. Other men in formal dress stand beside him.
stimulus.source_note: Signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact, Quai d'Orsay, Paris, August 27, 1928. French press photograph (Bibliothèque nationale de France); public domain.

source: original; stimulus photograph, signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact, Paris, 1928, public domain
stem: More than sixty nations signed the pact shown in the photograph. That wide support best shows which of the following?

options.text: Most nations were ready to disband their armies
options.misconception: No nation disbanded its army; the pact only renounced war on paper.

options.text: The League of Nations had become all-powerful
options.misconception: The League could not even stop Japan in Manchuria, and the United States was not a member.

options.text: The United States had joined the League of Nations
options.misconception: The United States never joined the League; the pact was signed outside it.

options.text: Many nations hoped treaties could outlaw war

rationales.A: Background from the books: the pact asked nations to renounce war, not to give up their armies.
rationales.B: Background from the books: the League had no army and no power to enforce its protests.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States stayed out of the League.
rationales.D: After the First World War, dozens of nations shared the hope that a treaty could cure war itself.
rationales.general:
1. The photograph shows a signing ceremony in Paris in 1928.
2. More than sixty nations eventually signed the pact renouncing war.
3. That breadth shows a shared hope after the First World War, not shared power.
4. The hope rested on the belief that war was a misunderstanding treaties could cure, a belief the 1930s would destroy.
Remember: wide agreement on paper is not the same as power to enforce it.
